value: Makes the main diagnosis that an open transaction (most likely left by the OOM-killed producer) holds the last stable offset (LSO) of the 3 partitions, so read_committed consumers cannot read past it, and that a transaction still open hours after the 60-second default transaction.timeout.ms (and far past the 15-minute transaction.max.timeout.ms) is hanging: the coordinator is not going to abort it.
reason: The cited consumer_config.html:294 and producer_config.html:1103-1107 (default 60000 ms) support this; the old text also demanded the read_uncommitted contrast, which is evidence, not the finding.

forceTerminateTransaction aborts the transaction the coordinator tracks for that transactional.id (TransactionsCommand.java:267, 'Force abort an ongoing transaction'); a hanging transaction is by definition one the coordinator no longer tracks on that partition (find-hanging logic, TransactionsCommand.java:672-691), so it is the same mechanism m5 says may not help and is not a correct alternative to abort --start-offset.
m4 is deleted, so m3 stands alone as the essential unblock step.

value:
The three partitions are blocked by an open transaction. A read_committed consumer only returns records up to the last stable offset, one less than the offset of the first open transaction, so it stops there; the audit consumer (read_uncommitted) is not limited and reads to the end. The killed ledger-writer pod most likely left a transaction open on those partitions. The coordinator aborts a transaction after the producer's transaction.timeout.ms (60 seconds by default), and no producer may ask for more than the broker's transaction.max.timeout.ms (15 minutes by default). A transaction still open after more than six hours is therefore hanging: the coordinator is not going to abort it. Confirm before changing anything: run kafka-transactions.sh describe-producers --topic ledger-events --partition

for each stuck partition and look at CurrentTransactionStartOffset, then kafka-transactions.sh find-hanging --topic ledger-events to list transactions open longer than the maximum timeout. kafka-transactions.sh describe --transactional-id shows what the coordinator still tracks for the killed pod's id. Then abort only what the tool found: kafka-transactions.sh abort --topic ledger-events --partition

--start-offset . Fixing the crash-looping pod also matters, because a producer that initialises with the same transactional.id aborts its predecessor's in-flight transaction, but that may not clear a transaction the coordinator no longer tracks. Verify that consumer lag on the three partitions starts to fall. The Kafka documentation on disk does not describe this procedure; the commands come from the tool's help.
reason: kafka_config.html:917 says the broker returns an error for a larger timeout, it does not cap it; the old reference said 'caps'.

value:
The read_committed consumers stop at the last stable offset, which a transaction left open by the killed producer holds. At more than six hours it is far past the 60-second default transaction timeout and the 15-minute broker maximum, so the coordinator will not abort it: it is hanging. Confirm without changing anything: kafka-transactions.sh --bootstrap-server find-hanging --topic ledger-events lists the open transactions with their StartOffset. Abort each one it lists with kafka-transactions.sh abort --topic ledger-events --partition

--start-offset , then watch the lag on the three partitions fall.
reason: The old alternative relied on forceTerminateTransaction (m4, deleted); this one reaches m1, m2 and m3 by another documented route (find-hanging, TransactionsCommand.java:545-575).

value: Strimzi 1.3.1, namespace data-int. Our KafkaConnect etl-connect (3 replicas) has run for a year; a CI pipeline creates and updates its 9 connectors through the Connect REST API. KafkaConnect etl-connect is Ready. What is wrong, which checks tell the possible causes apart, and what should we watch out for when we move the other 9 connectors this week?
reason: From memory of the operator code (not on disk, unverified): a KafkaConnector whose KafkaConnect lacks the annotation gets a NotReady condition, so 'no status at all' points to an unwatched namespace, which the Ready etl-connect rules out; the new wording fits either behaviour.

value: The most likely cause is that etl-connect does not have the annotation strimzi.io/use-connector-resources: "true". Without it the Cluster Operator does not manage KafkaConnector resources for that Connect cluster, so crm-sink is never created. Check with kubectl get kafkaconnect etl-connect -n data-int -o yaml, and read crm-sink's conditions. Less likely causes, with their checks: the KafkaConnector label must name the KafkaConnect (etl-connect, not the Kafka cluster) and the resource must be in the Connect cluster's namespace; and the Cluster Operator must watch data-int (STRIMZI_NAMESPACE in its Deployment), which the Ready status of etl-connect already suggests. The order matters for the migration. Strimzi's switch procedure is: first deploy KafkaConnector resources for every connector, then enable the annotation. If you enable it before the resources exist, the operator deletes all connectors, which here means the nine created by CI. So write KafkaConnectors for all nine, each named exactly like the existing connector (the resource name becomes the connector name) and with its current configuration (GET /connectors/<name>/config), apply them, then annotate etl-connect in Git. After that, the CI pipeline must stop using the REST API, because the operator reverts manual REST changes. Verify that metadata.generation equals status.observedGeneration and the cluster is Ready, that every KafkaConnector is Ready, and that GET /connectors lists all ten.
reason: Aligns the reference with the revised m3 (same names) and the revised question.

Only then add the annotation, stop the CI REST calls, and confirm with kubectl get kctr --selector strimzi.io/cluster=etl-connect that all ten are Ready.

value: We upgraded Argo CD from 2.13 to 3.6.1 last month; our Helm values for argocd-cm were carried over unchanged, including the resource tracking setting we had back then. Yesterday we renamed the Argo CD Application that deploys our Strimzi 1.3.1 Kafka resource from kafka-prod-app to prod, so that it matches the Kafka resource name prod. Since then the Application lists extra resources created by the Strimzi operator, among them the brokers' PersistentVolumeClaims, all marked as requiring pruning. Auto-sync has prune turned off. A colleague wants to run a sync with prune to clean up the view. What is going on and what should we do?
reason: From memory of the Argo CD controller (not on disk, unverified): resources with ownerReferences are not counted as an Application's top-level resources, and Strimzi sets ownerReferences on most operands (ref-certificates-and-secrets.adoc:344 for CA Secrets), so '60 Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, pods' is unlikely; PVCs without owner references are the realistic and the most dangerous case. The argo-cd proposal application-name-identifier.md:51 also ties the confusion to resources created 'without creating owner reference'.

value: Your argocd-cm still selects label tracking, the 2.x default; 3.0 changed the default to annotation tracking, but an explicit setting carried over wins. With label tracking, Argo CD considers resources labelled app.kubernetes.io/instance=<application name> to belong to that Application. Strimzi puts app.kubernetes.io/instance on what it creates, set to the name of the custom resource, prod. Renaming the Application to prod made Argo CD claim those resources; since they are not in Git, it wants to prune them. Do not sync with prune: it would delete operator-created resources such as the brokers' PVCs, and their data with them. Check first: kubectl get cm argocd-cm -n argocd -o yaml for application.resourceTrackingMethod, the labels of one of the listed resources (kubectl get pvc -n <ns> --show-labels), and argocd app diff. Fix by changing argocd-cm, in Git, to annotation tracking, then sync without prune so the Application's own resources receive the tracking annotation; the extra resources disappear from the view. If you cannot change the tracking method now, set a custom application.instanceLabelKey, or recreate the Application under its old name: an Application cannot be renamed in place, and argocd app delete cascades by default, so delete prod only with --cascade=false. Afterwards, confirm the Application lists only what is in Git.

value: The Job is a PreSync hook, and PreSync hooks run before Argo CD applies any of the Application's manifests. In a new environment that means the Kafka cluster and the KafkaUser orders-bootstrap do not exist yet, so the User Operator never creates the Secret orders-bootstrap, the Job's pod cannot start, and the sync waits for the hook indefinitely. Production works only because the Secret was created long ago. The Argo CD docs warn about exactly this: a PreSync hook that needs a Secret from the same Application fails on a fresh install. First stop the stuck operation with argocd app terminate-op orders-platform, and delete the leftover Job if it stays. Then change the repository: make the Job a PostSync hook, which runs after a successful sync with all resources Healthy, or a normal resource in a later sync wave than the KafkaUser. The other documented route is to keep the credentials outside this Application. Make the Job idempotent, because hooks run on every sync, and let it retry until the Secret exists, since the User Operator creates it shortly after the KafkaUser is applied. Verify with a fresh sync in the new environment.

value: Emptying broker 4 did not tell Strimzi which node to remove. When a node pool is scaled down, Strimzi removes the node with the highest ID unless the pool says otherwise, so with NODEIDS [3,4,5,6,7,8] and replicas 5 it tries to remove node 8. kafka-log-dirs.sh shows broker 8 still holding over 200 partition replicas, so the operator's scale-down check refuses and reports a warning; broker 4 sits empty. Fix it by choosing the node: annotate the KafkaNodePool brokers with strimzi.io/remove-node-ids="[4]" and keep replicas: 5, both in Git so whatever applies the repository does not revert it. The operator then removes node 4, which already holds nothing. Emptying broker 8 instead would remove node 8 and leave broker 4 on the hardware you want to retire. Before the change, confirm with kafka-log-dirs.sh that broker 4 is still empty. Do not use the skip-broker-scaledown-check annotation; removing broker 8 while it holds replicas would leave partitions under-replicated. Verify that NODEIDS no longer lists 4, five broker pods run, the warning is gone and no partition is under-replicated.

value: Run active/passive with a KafkaMirrorMaker2 in region B, close to its target: the Kafka docs recommend consuming from the remote cluster and producing to the local one, because a failed produce across regions is costlier than a failed fetch. With the default replication policy, topics appear in B with the source prefix, for example A.payments, and consumers in B must subscribe to those names. For resumption, run the checkpoint connector with sync.group.offsets.enabled so consumer offsets are committed in B while the groups are idle there, or translate offsets at failover with RemoteClusterUtils. Keep the consumers in B stopped until failover, and switch all members of a group together. Failback is a separate step: Strimzi advises against simply reversing the mirror, which duplicates records; rebuild A in a clean state, mirror all data from B to it with a new KafkaMirrorMaker2 using IdentityReplicationPolicy so names do not get a second prefix, remove the old A-to-B mirroring, and move clients back once A has caught up. On exactly-once: no. Offsets reach B with a lag, so after a failover some events are processed again whatever the mirroring mode, and Kafka documents exactly-once mirroring for dedicated MirrorMaker clusters, while the Strimzi docs say nothing about it for KafkaMirrorMaker2. Make the payment consumers idempotent or deduplicate by payment id. Numbers needed: RPO and RTO, peak throughput to mirror, inter-region bandwidth and latency, and acceptable lag.
reason: Aligns with the revised m3 and m4.

value: Mirror A to B with a KafkaMirrorMaker2 running in B and use RemoteClusterUtils at failover to translate each group's offsets and seek to them. Fail back by rebuilding A clean and mirroring everything from B to it with a new KafkaMirrorMaker2 using IdentityReplicationPolicy, then moving clients back. Mirroring cannot make failover exactly-once: offsets are translated with a lag, so some payments will be seen twice, and exactly-once is not documented for Strimzi's MirrorMaker 2; the payment consumers must deduplicate by payment id. Ask for RPO, RTO and the mirrored throughput.
reason: The old alternative's 'reverse mirror' is the failback Strimzi warns against (con-mm2-recovery.adoc:22-25).

value: The brokers' static value is ignored: with eligible leader replicas, on by default for clusters created on 4.1 or later, min.insync.replicas is a cluster-level config, created from the active controller's static config when it was missing (unset there, so 1), and broker-level values are removed. Change the existing cluster-level value with kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server <bootstrap> --entity-type brokers --entity-default --alter --add-config min.insync.replicas=2. Restarting the controllers with a new static value would not change it, because the cluster-level config is only added when none exists. Put the value in the controllers' properties for future clusters, check it with --entity-default --describe, and rerun the acceptance test.

KafkaNodePool brokers: resources requests and limits memory 16Gi, spec.jvmOptions: {gcLoggingEnabled: false}.
